title: Wanting, being able, having to
topic: vouloir, pouvoir, devoir + infinitive; il faut; polite requests
why: With vouloir, pouvoir, devoir and il faut, you can finally say what you want, what you can do and what you have to do. The lesson also gives you the polite formulas for asking a favor (Tu peux… ?, Je voudrais…) and flags the traps of English must and can.

{"lessons": ["

Vouloir, pouvoir, devoir

These three verbs are the engine of everyday conversation: what you want, what you can do, what you have to do. Like English “want to”, “can” and “must”, they're followed directly by an infinitive.

vouloirpouvoirdevoir
jeveuxpeuxdois
tuveuxpeuxdois
il, elle, onveutpeutdoit
nousvoulonspouvonsdevons
vousvoulezpouvezdevez
ils, ellesveulentpeuventdoivent

Look at the shape: the vowel changes in the singular and with ils (veu-, peu-, doi-), but nous and vous keep the vowel of the infinitive (voulons, pouvons, devons). The singular forms of vouloir and pouvoir end in -x with je and tu (je veux, tu peux), and all three singular forms sound the same.

Je veux sortir, mais je dois travailler.I want to go out, but I have to work.
Tu peux venir samedi ?Can you come on Saturday?

The negative

Ne… pas goes around the conjugated verb, and the infinitive comes after it: Je ne peux pas venir. (I can't come.) Elle ne veut pas sortir. (She doesn't want to go out.) Don't put pas after the infinitive.

The English “to” disappears: “I want to leave” is Je veux partir, with nothing between the two verbs. Never “je veux à partir”.

", "

Must, have to, can: the traps

Devoir and il faut

Devoir covers both “must” and “have to”: Je dois partir (I must leave, I have to leave). With a noun, it means “to owe”: Je dois dix euros à Paul (I owe Paul ten euros).

Il faut + infinitive expresses a general, impersonal obligation: “you have to”, “we need to”, “it's necessary to”. It never changes: there is only il faut, no other person.

Il faut réserver : le restaurant est petit.You have to book: the restaurant is small.
Il faut partir tôt demain.We need to leave early tomorrow.

Careful with the negative. Il ne faut pas and tu ne dois pas mean “you must not”, not “you don't have to”: Il ne faut pas fumer ici = You must not smoke here.

Pouvoir: can, may

Pouvoir is “can” in the sense of possibility and permission: Je peux venir à huit heures (I can come at eight), Je peux ouvrir la fenêtre ? (Can I open the window?). But for a skill you've learned (swimming, driving, cooking), French uses another verb, savoir, which you'll see in the next lesson.

Je ne peux pas venir : je suis malade.I can't come: I'm sick.
", "

Asking politely

To ask for a favor, use pouvoir as a question, exactly like English “Can you…?” With a friend, Tu peux… ?; with a stranger, a shopkeeper or several people, Vous pouvez… ?

FrenchEnglish
Tu peux porter le carton ?Can you carry the box?
Vous pouvez répéter, s'il vous plaît ?Could you repeat that, please?
Tu peux m'aider ?Can you help me?
On peut réserver une table ?Can we book a table?
Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.I'd like a coffee, please.

In Tu peux m'aider ?, m' means “me”: take the sentence as a fixed phrase for now. Je voudrais (I would like) is the polite formula for asking for something in a shop, a café or a hotel. Learn it as it is: it's a form of vouloir (the conditional) that you'll study in A2. Je veux (I want) is fine among friends but sounds blunt, even childish, with a waiter.

Answering

  • Yes: Oui, bien sûr ! (Yes, of course!), Pas de problème ! (No problem!)
  • No: Désolé, je ne peux pas. (a woman writes désolée), followed by a reason with devoir: Je dois travailler.
— Tu veux un café ? — Oui, je veux bien !— Do you want a coffee? — Yes, please!

Je veux bien is a soft, friendly yes: “I'd be glad to”, “yes, please”. It sounds much less demanding than a bare je veux.
